newsitem.title: UK: Pension funds to cut back on UK equities - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Pension funds to cut back on UK equities - analysts.

text.p: British pension funds may shift billions of pounds out of British equities and into gilts and overseas securities in reaction to new tax treatment, investment strategists say.

The abolition of the Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) credit for pension funds, announced in Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's budget, will level a playing field that until now made British shares the favoured investment for pension funds.
With pension fund assets totalling 560 billion stg, fund managers and actuaries are saying the effect of a change in allocation could be substantial.
"In a year, I wouldn't be surprised if (pension fund) holdings in equities fell by five or ten percent," said Andrew Smith of actuaries Bacon & Woodrow.
"That money will go into fixed income of some sort," he said.

The ACT credit allowed pension funds to claim back tax on 20 percent of dividends paid by UK companies, so its elimination makes those investments worth 20 percent less from a cash flow perspective, actuaries say.
"Its a more level playing field. An advantage UK equities had over other equity markets has been eliminated," said David Ross of Old Mutual Fund Managers, who manages a portfolio of $2 billion.

The investment pattern of pension funds based in the Isle of Man can serve as a proxy for UK pension funds, as they have never received an ACT credit but have sterling liabilities, according to Tony Osborne-Barker of consultants William M. Mercer.
Osborne-Barker says that Isle of Man funds typically invest 40 percent of their assets overseas, as opposed to 30 percent for UK funds.
This would imply an expatriation of some 50-60 billion stg in the long term, if British funds follow that pattern.
The end of the ACT credit will not necessarily result in pension funds dumping British equities wholesale, according to Ross.
"The UK equity market is still very attractive compared to others on most measures. (The abolition of ACT credit) takes away the icing but it doesn't take away the cake," he said.
Also, Ross said, pension funds benchmark themselves against their peers and are reluctant to step out of line lest their performance versus the group suffer.
Strong factors will drive pension funds to allocate more to fixed income, including an ageing workforce and a change in pension fund legislation, according to investment professionals.

Under changes to the Pensions Act introduced in April, British pension funds are now obliged to meet the Minimum Funding Requirement (MFR), which may tend to push up gilt holdings if a fund has an older member group, actuaries say.
"The MFR is going to drive asset allocation," said Osborne-Barker.
"All of the pressure is towards people moving towards gilts and away from equities," Ross said.
"Pension funds are getting more mature anyway, so asset liability models are telling them to increase fixed income."

British pension fund may decide to buy more corporate debt, Ross suggested, a market which may see more issuance as corporations recognise the higher cost of equity capital now that the ACT credit is gone.
"You are going to see a lower weight in equities, however you net the figures," said Andrew Smith.
